meta.name: Icelandic Sheepdog Grooming Guide
meta.excerpt: The Icelandic Sheepdog's thick double coat comes in long and short varieties and sheds significantly twice a year. This guide covers brushing, shedding management, and bathing for Iceland's only native breed.
meta.meta_description: Icelandic Sheepdog grooming guide: long vs short coat care, seasonal shedding, brushing routine, and bathing for this Nordic herding breed.

intro.label: Coat Overview
intro.heading: One Breed, Two Coat Lengths, Built for Iceland's Weather
intro.html:
Every Icelandic Sheepdog carries the same weatherproof double coat that let this spitz breed work Iceland's volcanic highlands for over a thousand years, but the breed comes in two distinct lengths that change how much time grooming actually takes. The short coat lies close and even over the whole body, while the long coat carries noticeably more volume — a fuller ruff around the neck, feathering down the back of the legs, a plumed tail that curls over the back, and fringing behind those alert, erect ears that frame the breed's characteristically foxy expression. Neither variety is low-maintenance exactly, but the short coat owner spends measurably less time at the brush than the long coat owner, and it's worth knowing which one you have before you commit to a grooming schedule you can't sustain.

Because this is a compact, sturdy dog in the 25–30 lb range rather than a large one, the total coat volume you're managing is smaller than what you'd deal with on a bigger northern breed — but the undercoat density is just as pronounced relative to body size. That dense undercoat is what insulated the breed through Icelandic winters while it drove semi-wild sheep down from the highlands each autumn, and it's the same undercoat that will end up on your couch twice a year if you don't stay ahead of it.

Puppy Coat to Adult Coat: What Changes and When

Icelandic Sheepdog puppies are born with a soft, fluffy single-layer coat that gives no hint of the grooming demands to come. Somewhere between 6 and 12 months, the adult double coat starts coming in underneath — a coarser, weather-resistant guard-hair layer growing in over the soft puppy fuzz that's being pushed out. This transition period is genuinely the most mat-prone stretch of the dog's life, more so than either seasonal shed later on, because you have two different hair textures tangling against each other simultaneously, especially behind the ears, in the neck ruff, and along the britches on the hind legs. Owners who skip brushing during this window because "the coat still looks fine" often find a solid mat behind each ear by month nine. Three brief brushing sessions a week through this stage, focused specifically on those friction zones, prevents the problem entirely and sets a routine the dog will accept for the next 12–14 years.

Once the adult coat is fully in — usually by 12 to 15 months, sometimes later on long-coat individuals — the texture settles into the classic double-coat pattern: a harsh, straight, weather-resistant outer coat over a soft, dense undercoat that does the real insulating work. From this point on, grooming is less about texture management and more about volume management, particularly around the two annual coat blows.

The Grooming Year at a Glance

Outside of shedding season, a healthy adult Icelandic Sheepdog in maintenance coat needs brushing two to four times a week depending on length, occasional baths, and routine nail, ear, and dental care — genuinely modest for a double-coated breed. The calendar changes sharply twice a year. Spring brings the release of the heavy winter undercoat as the dog transitions toward a lighter summer coat, and fall brings the reverse process as the winter undercoat grows back in ahead of cold weather. Each of these events runs 2 to 4 weeks and multiplies the amount of loose hair released daily by three or four times normal. Everything else in this guide — tools, bathing frequency, professional grooming timing — is built around planning for those two windows rather than being surprised by them.

care.label: Grooming Routine
care.heading: Building a Routine Around Two Shedding Seasons
care.html:
The baseline brushing schedule for the Icelandic Sheepdog splits by coat variety: short coats do well with two to three sessions a week, while long coats need three to four because the feathering on the legs, ears, and tail tangles faster than the flat body coat does. Work from the skin outward in sections rather than skimming the surface — a coat that looks smooth on top can be quietly matting at the base against the skin, and that's exactly where problems hide until they've tightened enough to require cutting out.

Tools Worth Owning

Three tools cover essentially everything this breed needs. A slicker brush ($12–$25) handles the body coat and breaks up loose undercoat on both varieties. A wide-tooth metal comb ($8–$15) is the tool that actually checks for hidden tangles in the feathering — run it through the leg fringe and behind the ears at every session, since this is where a slicker brush alone will miss developing mats. An undercoat rake ($15–$30) comes out specifically during the two annual coat blows; it's designed to pull dead undercoat out from beneath the guard coat without cutting the topcoat, so save it for shedding season rather than using it as a weekly tool, which would thin the weatherproof outer layer prematurely. A metal pin brush is a reasonable substitute for the slicker on the long-coat variety if you find the feathering pulls uncomfortably against a slicker's fine wire bristles.

Bath Protocol for a Double Coat

Bathe every 4 to 6 weeks with lukewarm water and a moisturizing dog shampoo — this breed's skin does fine without frequent washing, and over-bathing strips the same natural oils that make the coat weather-resistant in the first place. Work shampoo down to the skin rather than just over the topcoat, since the undercoat is where dirt and dander actually accumulate, then rinse thoroughly — shampoo residue left in a dense double coat is a common cause of itching that gets mistaken for allergies. Drying is the step people underestimate: towel-drying alone can leave the undercoat damp for hours, and a damp undercoat next to the skin is a setup for hot spots, especially in the folds behind the ears. A high-velocity dryer cuts drying time dramatically compared to air-drying and also helps blow out loose undercoat mechanically, which is why starting each shedding season with a bath-and-blowout combination shortens the overall shed considerably. If you don't own a high-velocity dryer, this single service is worth booking with a groomer even if you otherwise handle everything at home.

DIY vs. Professional Grooming: Realistic Costs

ServiceFrequencyTypical Cost
Home brushing session2–4x/weekNo cost after tools ($35–$70 total kit)
Home bathEvery 4–6 weeks$0 (shampoo ~$10–$15/bottle)
Professional bath and blowoutStart of each shedding season, 2x/year$40–$65
Full professional groomOptional, every 6–10 weeks$55–$90

Given the moderate size and manageable coat, most Icelandic Sheepdog owners handle the entire routine at home except for the seasonal blowout appointment, which is genuinely worth the money — a professional-strength dryer removes far more loose undercoat in one session than a week of home brushing.

Nails, Ears, Teeth, and the Double Dewclaws

Trim nails monthly; because this is an active, working-bred dog that's often exercised on soft trails and grass rather than pavement, nails frequently don't wear down naturally and grow long faster than owners expect. The erect, prick ears are a real advantage here compared to drop-eared breeds — there's better air circulation and much lower moisture retention, so a weekly visual check and occasional wipe is usually sufficient rather than the more intensive cleaning schedule floppy-eared dogs need. Brush teeth several times a week with an enzymatic dog toothpaste; periodontal disease is a common and preventable issue across all dog breeds, and it's one of the cheapest problems to head off with consistent home care. Finally, check the rear legs for double dewclaws, a breed-characteristic trait — many breeders remove them in puppyhood, but if yours are intact, they need monthly trimming of their own since they never touch the ground and never wear down on their own.

special.label: Special Considerations
special.heading: Feathering, Heat Sensitivity, and Where Owners Go Wrong
special.html:
Two things separate Icelandic Sheepdog grooming from a generic double-coat routine: the long coat's feathering, and the breed's Nordic build that makes it genuinely uncomfortable — not just less enthusiastic — in hot weather.

Feathering Is Where Mats Actually Start

On the long coat variety, the feathering behind the ears, down the back of the front legs, along the britches, and through the tail plume is thinner and softer than the body coat, which makes it tangle faster and hide small mats more effectively. A body coat mat is usually visible on sight; a mat forming in the ear feathering can go unnoticed for a week because it's tucked against the skull where you're not looking unless you deliberately part the fur. Make the metal comb, not the slicker brush, your tool for these specific zones at every session — run it all the way to the skin behind each ear and through the leg fringe, not just across the surface. A tangle caught early takes thirty seconds to work loose with fingers and a comb; the same tangle left for two more weeks tightens against the skin and can only be removed by shaving that patch, which on a long-coat dog leaves an obvious bald spot that takes months to blend back in.

Built for Cold, Not Heat

The Icelandic Sheepdog's entire coat structure evolved for a subarctic island climate, and that shows up directly in how the dog handles a hot summer. Exercise in the cooler parts of the day during warm months rather than midday, and provide shade and water generously — this is not a breed that self-regulates well in heat the way some short-coated dogs do. The instinct to shave the coat down for summer relief is understandable but counterproductive: the double coat insulates against heat gain from the sun almost as effectively as it insulates against cold, and shaving it off removes that protection while exposing pale skin to sunburn. Regrowth after shaving is also frequently uneven on this breed, sometimes leaving a patchy, cottony texture that never quite matches the original coat. The correct response to summer heat is more frequent brushing to keep the undercoat thinned out naturally, not clippers.

Grooming Mistakes That Come Up Repeatedly

  • Bathing too often "to control shedding." Extra baths don't reduce shedding meaningfully and do wash out the natural oils this breed's coat relies on for weatherproofing, leading to a drier, itchier coat that actually sheds more.
  • Running the undercoat rake year-round instead of just during coat blows. Used constantly rather than seasonally, it thins the protective guard-hair topcoat that's supposed to shed water and block wind.
  • Assuming erect ears mean no ear care needed. The prick ears do reduce moisture problems compared to drop-eared breeds, but debris still collects and a weekly check is still worth the two minutes it takes.
  • Ignoring the double rear dewclaws. Because they never contact the ground, these nails can curl into the pad if left untrimmed — a painful, avoidable injury.
  • Ordering a full clip-down at the groomer for a "low-maintenance summer look." This backfires on any double-coated Nordic breed, this one included, for the heat-regulation reasons above.

When Coat Care Signals a Health Issue

Occasionally what looks like a grooming problem is actually a health one. A dull, thinning, or unusually slow-regrowing coat outside the normal shedding calendar is worth mentioning to your veterinarian rather than assuming it's just seasonal — thyroid changes and skin conditions can present first as coat quality changes in dogs of this breed's age and lifespan (typically 12–14 years), and catching them early through routine grooming observation is one of the genuine benefits of staying hands-on with the coat rather than outsourcing it entirely.

faq.q: Does the Icelandic Sheepdog need professional grooming?
faq.a: Not as a strict requirement — most of the routine (brushing, monthly baths, nails, ears) is manageable at home. Where a professional visit earns its cost is the start of each shedding season: a bath followed by a high-velocity blowout pulls out loose undercoat far faster than a week of home brushing and noticeably shortens how long the shed drags on.

faq.q: How often does an Icelandic Sheepdog actually shed?
faq.a: There's light, steady shedding year-round, but the real volume comes twice a year during coat blows — once in spring and once in fall — when the dense undercoat releases over a 2 to 4 week window. During these stretches, expect three to four times the normal amount of loose hair and plan on daily brushing until it tapers off.

faq.q: Is the long coat or short coat easier to maintain?
faq.a: The short coat is noticeably lower-maintenance day to day, needing about two to three brushings a week versus three to four for the long coat. The long coat's feathering behind the ears and along the legs is where most mats start, so it demands more deliberate comb work at each session even though total shedding volume between the two varieties is similar.

faq.q: Why shouldn't I shave my Icelandic Sheepdog in summer?
faq.a: The double coat regulates temperature in both directions — it blocks heat gain from the sun almost as well as it blocks cold. Shaving removes that protection, exposes the skin to sunburn, and often grows back uneven or cottony on this breed. Managing summer heat is better done with more frequent brushing, shade, water, and exercising during cooler hours, not clippers.

faq.q: What should I do about my Icelandic Sheepdog's double rear dewclaws?
faq.a: If your dog still has them (many breeders remove them in puppyhood), trim them on the same monthly schedule as the regular nails. Because dewclaws never touch the ground, they don't wear down naturally, and if neglected they can curl around and grow into the paw pad, causing pain and infection.
